newsitem.title: USA: Death rattle at high court.
newsitem.headline: Death rattle at high court.

text.p: James Lee moved away from a small band of shouting, singing demonstrators on Wednesday as the Supreme Court heard arguments on doctor-assisted suicide.
Struggling to roll his wheelchair up a handicapped ramp next to the front steps of the court on a frigid, sunny day, Lee wanted to get away from the bull-horn noise.
"I'm against it too, but I can't take all that shouting," the disabled veteran from Memphis said as he rolled away.

"Not Dead Yet!" -- the name of a Rochester, New York, based group at the event -- was the chant shouted by about 100 demonstrators opposed to proposals to legalise doctor-assisted suicide. Many were in wheel chairs and on crutches.
Only a handful showed up to lobby for the other side.
Although the whole court demonstration was minuscule by Washington standards, more than 120 reporters and scores of police were on hand.
Reporters scurried around looking for home-town angles. "Anyone here from Michigan?" one inquired.
A priest roamed through the thicket of television reporters, asking, "Do you need a sound bite?"
After an all-night vigil at a nearby church, organisers set up louspeakers outside the granite-faced court.
A folk-singing group of women from Toledo, Ohio, entertained them with songs that included such lyrics as, "We are not yet dead people, and we are scared for our lives."

"We want to live!" shouted Carol Clay from Chicago, a demonstration leader. She was trying to stir the immobile crowd, which included a silent quartet of supporters of the Washington area Hemlock Society who held up a banner favouring death-ending measures for the terminally ill.

Clay boasted that she once joined a group of fellow believers on a trip to confront "death doctor" Jack Kevorkian, America's best-known advocate and practitioner of medically assisted suicide, who has publicly acknowledged attending more than 40 deaths since 1990.
"We went to Kevorkian's home and we sure kicked some tush that day," Clay told the milling crowd.

A woman in a wheelchair sporting a sticker reading "Too Sexy For My Wheelchair" handed out blood red-circulars reading: "First they call us names, then they say we have no quality of life. Then we're dead."
"If the Supreme Court declares mercy death legal, they'll declare open season on 43 million (disabled) Americans," it declared.

Out of earshot of the determined little crowd, Justice Clarence Thomas rocked quietly in his high-backed leather chair, sipping from his pewter water goblet as he studied the frescoes below the domed ceiling. He listened quietly for over two hours as lawyers debated the issue.

Not so his eight colleagues who fired questions at lawyers who used such ominous language as "charlatans and doctors of death operating in the shadows" or "the final chapter of life" as they argued the pros and cons of legalising assisted suicide.
Like most of her colleagues, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wondered if a court ruling would change much. After all, she asked at one point, "is all of this a great sham?"
"Anyone with enough sophistication can end their life," she said.
